title: What a Computer Really Does
subtitle: Strip away the apps, the windows, the AI — underneath, a computer is doing one stupefyingly simple thing, billions of times a second.
hook: A modern laptop can render a movie, run a game, and hold a video call at once. It feels impossibly clever. But underneath every bit of that is a machine doing something almost embarrassingly simple: **fetch an instruction, do it, repeat.** No magic, no understanding — just a mindless loop run so fast that intelligence *appears*. Today's lesson is the bedrock of this whole track: once you see the loop, every layer above it — operating systems, databases, the cloud — becomes a story about hiding that simplicity behind useful lies.

sections.heading: The whole machine, in one loop
sections.body:
At the center of a computer is the **CPU**. It does nothing but repeat a cycle called **fetch–decode–execute**:

1. **Fetch** the next instruction from memory.
2. **Decode** what it means (add? compare? jump?).
3. **Execute** it — usually a tiny operation on a couple of numbers.

Then it does it again. And again. A few billion times per second. Every program you've ever run is just a long list of these micro-instructions. The CPU has no idea it's "running a browser" — it only ever sees the next instruction.

sections.caption: The loop that runs everything. The Program Counter tracks where you are; each turn fetches one instruction, decodes it, executes it, and advances.
sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    PC["Program Counter\npoints at next instruction"] --> F["FETCH\nread instruction\nfrom memory"]
    F --> D["DECODE\nwhat operation?"]
    D --> E["EXECUTE\ndo it (add, compare, jump...)"]
    E --> U["advance / update PC"]
    U --> PC

sections.label: The one idea to keep
sections.body: Speed plus simplicity *looks* like intelligence. The CPU is dumb; it's just fast and relentless. Everything that feels smart about computers is built on stacking simple, reliable operations — a theme we'll hit again and again in this track.

sections.heading: Why we build 'abstraction layers'
sections.body:
No human writes billions of raw CPU instructions by hand. So we build **layers**, each hiding the messy layer below and offering something friendlier:

- **Machine code** (raw instructions) →
- **Programming languages** (Python, C) that compile down to it →
- **Operating systems** that manage memory and hardware for you →
- **Applications** you actually click on.

Each layer is a *useful lie*: it lets you ignore the details underneath so you can think bigger. When you write `print("hi")`, you're standing on a tower of abstractions that eventually becomes fetch–decode–execute. Almost all of software engineering is choosing the right layer to think at — and knowing that a real, simple machine is always at the bottom.

sections.caption: A short, concrete walk through the fetch–execute cycle — what the CPU is literally doing each tick.

takeaways: A CPU endlessly repeats one loop: **fetch → decode → execute**.
Every program is just a long list of these tiny instructions; the CPU never sees the 'big picture'.
Apparent intelligence comes from **simple operations run incredibly fast**, not from cleverness.
Software is built as **abstraction layers**, each hiding the one below (machine code → languages → OS → apps).
Good engineering is picking the right layer to think at — while remembering a simple machine sits at the bottom.

quiz.q: What are the three steps of the CPU's core cycle, in order?
quiz.explain: Fetch the next instruction, decode what it means, execute it — then repeat, billions of times a second.

quiz.q: Why do we say each abstraction layer is a 'useful lie'?
options: It hides the messy layer below so you can think at a higher level
It runs slower but looks nicer
It stores false data for security
It only works on some computers
quiz.explain: Each layer lets you ignore the details beneath it. `print("hi")` hides a whole tower that ends in raw CPU instructions.

quiz.q: Where does a computer's apparent 'intelligence' actually come from?
options: Simple operations executed extremely fast and reliably
quiz.explain: The CPU is 'dumb' — it just does one tiny thing at a time, but so fast and so reliably that intelligence emerges from the stack above it.
